extracted_by: hand, T-0310 — the Democrat read, January 1834
note: Vol. I No. 10, and it carries the month's centrepiece: the list of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 1 January 1834, ninety-seven names over John S. C. Hogan's signature. Beside it, two church buildings in use — the Presbyterian meeting house dedicated the week before and a Baptist meeting house hosting School District No. 2's trustee election — a civil marriage before the county clerk, a lumber yard being got ready for the opening of navigation, and four storefronts placed against one another down what is almost certainly one block of South Water Street.

claims.notes:
THE PEOPLE OF CHICAGO ON 1 JANUARY 1834, AS THE POST OFFICE HAD THEM. Ninety-seven listed names and the postmaster, in a town of a few hundred — the single densest record of who was here that this corpus holds for the year before the scene date, and RULING 1 APPLIES IN FULL: this is Chicago's own post office, so every listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged `letter_list_only`. (Contrast the August 1834 'List of Letters', which is Hennepin's reprinted and mints nobody.)

THE HAND COUNT, which the ticket requires stated. Counted by eye off the printed list as the transcription preserves it: line 1113 carries 16 names, 1115 six, 1117 one, 1119 six, 1121 one, 1123 six, 1125 sixty, 1127 one — **97 personal names, plus John S. C. Hogan's signature as postmaster**, which is the 98 entities this claim carries. THAT IS THE COUNT THE TRANSCRIPTION SUPPORTS AND NOT NECESSARILY THE COUNT THAT WAS PRINTED. The .docx extraction has crushed the printed list's two alphabetical columns into eight paragraph lines, interleaving them, and it has left orphan debris where names were — 'Me print ofl Coram amor Hei otinan Wor in vard' at 1111, 'pe see' at 1117, 'onger areita' and 'Thomas OF ae 3' at 1119, 'if 1 LabiteLase Cemier Go Bene' at 1121, 'ef' at 1123 — every one of which stood where a name or part of one stood. So 97 is a FLOOR, the loss is visible rather than estimated, and closing the gap needs the page images. Filed as a ticket.

WHAT WAS NOT DONE. Fragments are minted as fragments: 'William Cr[…]', 'Gustavus C[…]', 'Benj. Cl[…]', 'Lewis Tem[…]' keep their cut surnames rather than being completed into likely Chicago names, and bare surnames with no initial ('[?] Gay', '[?] Warren', '[?] Gooding') are minted with the marker rather than joined to anybody already in the gazetteer. The trailing digits in the print ('J. W. Lewis 2', 'H. S. Bennett 2', 'William Elliot 3') are the count of letters waiting and are read as such, not as part of a name. NO MERGES ARE DECLARED out of this list, including the several names that resemble 1835 residents — an initial is often the only thing separating two members of one family, which is the rule identity.json states.

claims.notes: THE PRESBYTERIAN MEETING HOUSE IS IN USE AS THE TOWN'S PUBLIC ROOM one week after its dedication was reported (1834-01-21, claim c002 there). A temperance society meeting in it at six in the evening on a Thursday in January means a building that can be lit and warmed and that holds an audience — which is more than the dedication notice alone establishes. Together with the Baptist meeting house of claim c003, this issue documents TWO church buildings standing in Chicago in January 1834, both of them hosting civil meetings.

claims.notes: A LUMBER YARD AND A WAREHOUSE, ANNOUNCED FOR THE OPENING OF NAVIGATION 1834 — so this is a business under construction in the last days of 1833, intended to be standing when the ice went out. Two structures, not one: a yard for the lumber and a warehouse for commission and storage of provisions and groceries. And a supply chain, stated: an agent, Calvin Britain, at the mouth of the St. Joseph, through whom Michigan lumber is consigned — the same St. Joseph run the schooners of 1834 work (1834-08-06, claim c007 there). THE PROPRIETOR IS NOT SETTLED. The signature reads 'te. DAVID.' with the surname cut; a David Carver advertises lumber and auction in this corpus later in 1834, which makes him the obvious candidate and is exactly why the supply is left bracketed and out of the entities rather than written into the gazetteer.

claims.notes: A THIRD DOCUMENTED STOREFRONT ON THE SAME BLOCK, given against the second. Montgomery's boot and shoe shop is 'next door to P. Cohen's Store', and Cohen's store is at the east end of South Water Street by its own standing head (1834-01-07, claim c009) — so the chain places Montgomery there too, at one remove. The reading records the anchor and does NOT collapse the chain: the business's street is left null and the placement is `relative` on Cohen's store, because 'next door to a shop that advertises itself at the east end of a street' is one inference away from an address and this project keeps that distinction. The date '1835' in the print is read 1833 from the issue it stands in. THE SIGNATURE IS LOTON W. MONTGOMERY'S, AND THE SHOEMAKING IS NOT THE AUCTIONEER'S (T-1040). This is ONE standing advertisement — 'Boot & Shoe Making. The subscriber having recently commenced the above business, next door to P. Cohen's Store …', the same setting word for word under a dateline of Chicago, December 1833 — and the Democrat runs it from 17 December 1833 through at least 8 April 1834. Four impressions bear on the signature and three of them carry an L: it is set WHOLE as 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' at 1833-12-17 c003 and at 1834-04-08 c007, and the damaged 1834-03-04 c028 preserves the initial itself — its column reads 'L.      Mo}' where the name stood. Those impressions stand on both sides of the two that read 'W. MONTGOMERY' (1834-01-28 c008, and 1834-03-25 c009, whose initial its own note says was READ FROM the January printing rather than off its own page). So the reading is L. W. Montgomery throughout, and `as_printed` is left exactly as each column sets it. WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not a merge of 'W. Montgomery' with 'L. W. Montgomery'. This corpus carries a real W. Montgomery — the auctioneer and commission merchant of South Water Street, signing 'W. MONTGOMERY' and 'W. MONTGOMERY, Auc'r.' across the summer of 1835 — and the identity policy's families rule rightly refuses to join two Montgomerys on a differing initial. The discriminator here is not the initial; it is that the shoemaking notice and the auction notices are two different advertisements, and this one is the shoemaker's. Before this ruling `person_w_montgomery` carried 'boot and shoe maker' beside 'auctioneer', 'commission merchant', 'land agent' and 'newspaper agent' — one record holding two men's trades on two signatures separated on the page. Loton W. Montgomery is in this reconstruction under his own name (hh_montgomery_l_w), on the polls of 1834 and 1835 and in Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844, a shoemaker in each.

claims.notes: A TAVERN CHANGES HANDS, AND THE BUILDING IS 'THAT NOTED TAVERN STAND IN CHICAGO' — the definite article doing the work an address would. It was lately occupied by John W. Wattles and is renamed the Traveller's Home by its new keeper, whose own name the OCR has destroyed in the standing head and which is NOT supplied. For the reconstruction the useful part is the succession: a single well-known tavern building in the town, under a second keeper from October 1833, still advertising in January 1834 and again on 1834-01-21 (page 4, line 1165). Whether it is the same house as Graves's Tavern or the Chicago Hotel — the other two public houses this month names — is not said by any of the three and is not inferred.
